stories.headline: Seven things Solak thinks entering NFL Week 4
stories.summary: Bowers will go off under Klint Kubiak? The Rams need another pass catcher? Steelers-Browns will be fun? And Lamar Jackson for MVP? Get ready for Week 4 with some takes.
stories.body:
Who's ready to put their thinking caps on? Week 3 of the 2026 NFL season will go down in the history books, as 12 -- count 'em, 12! -- Sunday games finished within one score, the new single-day record for the league. Toss in two fun primetime games on Thursday and Monday and that was about as good a week as NFL football gets.

Every Tuesday of the NFL season, I'll turn the page from the previous week to the upcoming one with seven things I think. These aren't full-scale predictions; those come later. They aren't concrete takeaways from the past week of NFL action, either; those are fired off Sunday or Monday. Instead, these are the uncertain topics. They are things that might be true, but it'll probably take the next few games to find out. And at the bottom, you'll find a few extra half-thoughts ... just those little inklings I'm unable to shake.

This week, I'll start with the one player I've been most excited to see in his new system, make another pick for MVP (I'm up to two in three weeks) and highlight an intradivisional game between surprising 2-1 teams you should probably watch for fun. Here are seven things I think ahead of Week 4.

Jump to:

Bowers is the new JSN

Jackson for league MVP

Lawrence reminds us to be patient with QBs

Rams should make one more trade

Steelers-Browns is suddenly important

I will never trust the Bills

McCarthy won't save the Giants

Five extra inklings

I think ... Brock Bowers is the new Jaxon Smith-Njigba
We had to wait a few extra weeks for it, but one of the most anticipated debuts of the 2026 season struck Sunday. Bowers, the third-year Raiders tight end fresh off a meniscus cleanup, took his first snaps in Klint Kubiak's offense against the Saints. The final card? Ten catches, 116 yards and a score. Bowers has four career games of 10-plus receptions, 100-plus yards and a touchdown. Since he entered the league in 2024, the rest of the NFL's tight ends combined have only four such games.

So, he picked up where he left off.

Watching Bowers is such a delight. He has receiver-like instincts and catch technique. He has receiver-like movement skills. He can run receiver-esque routes -- routes other coaches wouldn't think to ask of their tight ends.

Now, you've likely heard other tight ends erroneously called "quasi-wide receivers." Analysts were obsessed with flex tight ends in the prime of Travis Kelce and Mark Andrews, so we started throwing the label around willy-nilly. It's important, in our appreciation of what Bowers brings to the Raiders' offense, to be objective about the uniqueness of his impact.

Think of a smaller pass-catching tight end who's having a productive year: Dalton Kincaid with the Bills has been a breakout star. Against the Lions in Week 2, Kincaid had seven targets from traditional wide receiver alignments -- either in the slot or wide -- which was one of the highest among all tight ends this season. Arizona's Trey McBride, the league's preeminent move tight end, had 10 such targets against the Seahawks in Week 2 and the Chargers in Week 1.

Bowers had 13 on Sunday against the Saints. In fact, all 13 of his targets were from slot or wide alignments. It's the most such targets a tight end has seen in the past three seasons. Specifically out wide, Bowers was targeted eight times, which ties the most out-wide targets a tight end has had since the 2016 season -- as far back as I have alignment data. He caught six passes out wide ... which ties the most out-wide receptions a tight end has had since the 2016 season.

That is wide receiver usage. The Raiders were in "multi-tight-end" sets on 81% of their snaps Sunday -- the highest rate for any team in a game this season -- because they're not actually multi-tight-end sets. It's really 11.5 personnel, because they have the skeleton key in Bowers.

Let's see what this looks like in practice. On a key third down late in the third quarter of Sunday's win, the Raiders isolate Bowers on the backside by motioning to a four-strong formation. With all four receivers to the opposite side of the field, the Saints' hands are tied -- they have to play Bowers in man coverage with their best man corner, Kool-Aid McKinstry. Watch Bowers feint the slant, and when McKinstry doesn't bite, he bursts to McKinstry's upfield shoulder to threaten the go-ball and open up space for the back-shoulder throw. It's short, because Kirk Cousins underappreciated Bowers' speed, and Bowers makes a great adjustment for the first down.

This is obviously super-duper sick. For most teams, a tight end in isolation on a cornerback is not a win -- for the Raiders, it is.

What's particularly cool is that Kubiak wants to give these opportunities to Bowers over anyone else on the Raiders' roster. Last season, that player for Kubiak was Smith-Njigba, the Seahawks' star receiver. We see almost the exact same play here, in the Seahawks' 2025 Week 7 game against the Texans. Sam Darnold alerts to the man coverage on the backside and throws Smith-Njigba on the vertical route against press coverage, keeping the ball vertical instead of throwing it to the back shoulder given the positioning of the corner.

This is far from the only example we can find of Bowers getting the JSN treatment from Kubiak. Again in isolation on the backside of the formation and again on third down, Bowers uses his reduced alignment to get into an out-breaking route at the sticks. Smith-Njigba was used on similar routes in similar alignments for Kubiak on money downs last season.

Here, Bowers motions into a stack alignment to get a free release into an option route -- look at how easily he widens McKinstry before snapping back into space. He has special burst and body control for a tight end, much as Smith-Njigba has special burst and body control for a wide receiver. Smith-Njigba takes the option route the other direction, but the usage is the same.

The fact that Kubiak is giving Bowers the same plays he gave Smith-Njigba is important because Smith-Njigba was as high volume a receiver as we had seen in decades. Smith-Njigba had a preposterous 44.1% of the Seahawks' receiving yards and 35.9% of the Seahawks' targets through the 2025 season -- the highest share of a team's receiving production since 2012 Brandon Marshall. In one game, Bowers had 46.8% of the team's receiving yards and 41.9% of the team's targets. That's Smith-Njigba usage and Smith-Njigba volume.

Of course, because Bowers is a tight end, he won't get the same explosive opportunities that Smith-Njigba got down the field. JSN had a heavy dose of crossing patterns that Bowers largely didn't see in Week 3 -- those are big-play run-after-catch chances of play-action. Smith-Njigba could also outrun a corner for a 50-yard vertical, and Bowers isn't doing that.

But what he is doing, we haven't seen at the tight end position since Kelce -- fitting, given the Raiders (3-0) face the Chiefs (3-0) in Week 4. Bowers now has two career games with at least six targets or at least five receptions from wide alignments -- games we could reasonably call "high volume" games on the outside. He is only 30 games into his NFL career. Kelce has played in 168 games since 2016. If Bowers' Week 3 usage keeps up, he'll join prime Kelce as the lone tight end of this era who lines up on the outside and wins, over and over again.

It will be interesting to see how the Chiefs handle this. Through three weeks, they have played two teams without a strong tight end feature -- the Broncos (2-1) and the Dolphins (0-3), with the Colts (1-2) and Tyler Warren sandwiched there in the middle. Warren went for 21 yards on six catches (seven targets) in that Indy game, as the Colts have devolved into targeting him shallow on designed touches to protect the recovering Daniel Jones from long dropbacks. Bowers will be the Chiefs' first real tight end test.

Now, Bowers isn't always going to have an 80% target rate on his out-wide alignments -- the Saints' corners were playing far too off Bowers to start the game. He isn't always going to catch and win all those isolation routes, either. But I imagine we're only at the top of Kubiak's bag with Bowers. Kubiak's greatest wizardry, among his many achievements in 2025, was how he stayed ahead of defensive adjustments and always found a way to manufacture opportunities for Smith-Njigba. It's time to see whether he can encore that performance with his star tight end.

I think ... Lamar Jackson is the league MVP
Two weeks ago, I thought Trevor Lawrence was the league MVP. Do I still think that? Yep. Jackson is, too. I get to have multiple MVPs. It's Week 3, which means there should be 17 MVPs so far. It's also my column, and I'll do what I want.

Anyway, here's the Ravens' go-ahead touchdown late in the fourth quarter against the Cowboys on Sunday, which put Baltimore up 31-28 with 1:30 left. It's an easily forgotten play given the Cowboys' ensuing score, then the remarkable last-second win by the Ravens -- but it's important. Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle dialed up a nice snag concept from three tight ends in the low red zone, and he gets a bust from the Cowboys' defense. Two defenders run with rookie tight end Josh Cuevas (No. 85), leaving fellow rookie tight end Matthew Hibner (No. 88) open on the snag route for just a moment.

Only ... he's not open. Linebacker Jaishawn Barham (No. 55), who initially looked to be pressuring, is lurking off the line of scrimmage and ready to pounce on the ball. If Jackson throws this ball fast to Hibner, who appears to be open, Barham has a great chance to pluck it out of the air and end the game.

So Jackson gives the slightest little pump, and while pumping, pulls Barham a little further toward Hibner. There's a free rusher in Jackson's face, but the threat of the QB's escapability delays the rush. Now he can reload quickly (Jackson's pump fakes are particularly devastating because he has a compact release and can get out of his pumps wicked fast) and throw a softball over Barham while pulling Hibner away from coverage.

This play looks so easy and so simple -- but only because Jackson makes it so. At times his calm, almost lackadaisical style generates some devastating turnovers. But it also allows him to create throws like this -- Hibner is rarely the primary target on this play -- with his unique blend of dual-threat ability, arm talent and coverage recognition. This is a special play masquerading as a routine one.

Jackson was predictably effective against a banged-up Cowboys secondary, and any argument against his MVP candidacy would highlight that two of the three defenses he has played (Colts and Cowboys) are particularly poor units. That's fine. I'd be quick to point out that Zay Flowers was available for only 15 routes against the Cowboys, and the Ravens have filled his absence with players such as Devontez Walker and Chris Moore. Receiver depth is killing them, and still Jackson is making the passing game work with Rashod Bateman and an aging Mark Andrews.

I'd also point out that the Ravens were on their third center in this game -- rookie guard Olaivavega Ioane had to kick inside and snap following injuries to Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic -- and that the Ravens' short-yardage rushing attack, which should be a strength of a team featuring Derrick Henry, continues to fail them in key moments. Henry was stuffed on two fourth-and-1 runs in this game and took a tackle for loss on a third-and-1 that forced a punt. Let's not even start on the defense, which is allowing 3.1 points per drive in the second half (tied for fifth worst in the league).

Jackson is holding together an offense that is predictably volatile in its first three games of a complex Doyle system. Jackson is accounting for serious personnel deficiencies on the interior and at pass catcher. This is what elite quarterbacks do, and it's what MVPs do.

The Ravens (2-1) have a reasonable upcoming schedule -- vs. Titans, at Falcons, at Browns -- to iron out their operational wrinkles. Coach Jesse Minter projected long-term absences for both Gwyn (ankle) and Pocic (knee), leaving Baltimore scrambling for a center or guard solution. Will it trade for Jake Andrews or Garrett Bradbury? Or maybe sign Kevin Zeitler and kick Ioane in to center permanently? All of the solutions are imperfect and will require time to jell.

Things get serious with games vs. the Bengals, at the Bills and vs. the Jaguars. That run might put up Jackson against Joe Burrow, Josh Allen and Lawrence -- three other AFC quarterbacks who might have serious MVP résumés by that time. These head-to-head matchups will have big ripple effects not just on conference playoff seeding but on the race for football's biggest individual award.

I think ... Trevor Lawrence is the ultimate reminder of quarterback patience
I implored you in this very column last week to chill out about Patriots quarterback Drake Maye. He rewarded me with three of the worst decisions I've ever seen him make. Nice call!

In the same column, I listed everything I found wrong and offensive about the Chargers -- Justin Herbert included. In Week 3, the defense took the ball away from the Bills five times and the Chargers still lost for all the reasons I listed last week -- Herbert, once again, included. His pick in the end zone to C.J. Gardner-Johnson is more offensive to me than Maye's pick to Travis Hunter ... but only just.

What do we do about this? Two Terminator quarterbacks -- huge frames, big arms, supercomputer processing, deadly accurate and tough as steel -- are collapsing into piles of nuts and bolts (I've never seen the Terminator movies, I don't know what they're actually made of) before our eyes. How do we parse this?

First, we need to remember that development is not linear. The greatest annual truth in the NFL is that players don't get progressively better or worse in discrete fashion. The temptation, after Maye's tremendous Year 2, is to expect him to keep getting better in Year 3 because that's what young quarterbacks typically do between Years 2 and 3.

But quarterbacks change like the weather. It will get colder across the end of September and into October, then again across November and December. But the temperature doesn't fall by a degree a day. There are unseasonably warm weeks. There are nippy mornings and sunny afternoons. The trend is better appreciated through the wider lenses of weeks and months.

Let me give you a counterexample to Herbert and Maye: Trevor Lawrence. The Jaguars quarterback is a helpful analog to Maye and Herbert because the three are quite similar stylistically. All have big frames and prefer to stay in the pocket to make aggressive throws. All have made more hay in their careers hitting tougher downfield windows than peppering underneath options. All can withstand contact, break the pocket and create with their legs. Since Maye entered the league as a rookie in 2024, all three quarterbacks are among the top 10 quarterbacks in air yards to the sticks and among the bottom 10 in the rate of their throws behind the line of scrimmage.

Lawrence is a fire-breathing dragon right now. He shoots from the hip, ripping his first read into tight coverage windows with the arm arrogance of Brett Favre. Since Week 9 of last season -- after the Jaguars' bye and midseason acquisition of receiver Jakobi Meyers -- Lawrence leads the league in the percentage of his throws that are at least 10 yards downfield (42.1%). This sort of play style invites high peaks and low valleys -- more so than with quarterbacks such as Joe Burrow or Bo Nix or Jared Goff, who are all more willing to take what is given by the defense. This is not a commentary on who is better. It's about how they play.

Lawrence has found supporting contributors to sustain his peaks and minimize his valleys. Star wide receiver Parker Washington has preposterous play strength and a wonderful catch radius. Just look at this touchdown from the Jaguars' drubbing of the Patriots this past Sunday -- a silly snag.

In second-year head coach Liam Coen, Lawrence has found a play designer who is not adept at getting him good pre-snap keys with motion and formation. Coen's excellent screen game and deep bag of tricky run concepts gives the Jaguars' offense that steady heartbeat it desperately needs; it creates the 5-, 6-yard gains necessary to stay on track and protect field position, such that Lawrence can be the big-armed playmaker he's already predisposed to be.

Lawrence's play style hasn't changed much over the years -- but his effectiveness has, and it has much to do with his environment. Take just last season: to start the 2025 season, the Jaguars were an operational mess that rivaled that of the 2026 Chargers, and they had personnel issues that rivaled that of the 2026 Patriots.

Through three weeks, the 2025 Jaguars led the league with 21 offensive penalties -- the 2026 Chargers lead the league currently with 20. Receiver Brian Thomas Jr. led the 2025 Jaguars with 109 routes and 25 targets through three weeks (somehow with only seven catches) -- behind him on the receiver depth chart was Hunter (80 routes) and Dyami Brown (78). Through three weeks, in the absence of A.J. Brown, the 2026 Patriots' leading target getters are Mack Hollins (16), DeMario Douglas (14) and Romeo Doubs (11), the free agent addition who has failed to contribute as expected for his $19 million contract.

I would argue that quarterbacks coded like Lawrence, Herbert and Maye -- more willing to trust their arm, test coverage, put all of their chips on one big bet -- are more obviously affected by circumstance than the more cautious quarterbacks. They already want to hang in the pocket, so when their bad offensive lines fail, they're late to escape and collect too many hits. They want to make tight-window throws, so when they play with poor receivers rooms, they're asking imperfect players to make high-difficulty plays.

Perhaps it's not play style but pigheadedness. Herbert, Maye, Lawrence -- they're all stubborn. They don't adjust their internal clock as quickly as other quarterbacks do. They don't hasten to get the ball to the checkdown when their downfield receivers are losing and accordingly minimize yards after catch. Risk management is a legitimate skill for quarterbacks -- one that Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen have learned well over their ascension into elite quarterback status. They started their careers as flamethrowers and have learned (to varying degrees) how to play more methodical ball. Maybe Maye and Herbert will learn that lesson this season, and when they do, their play will suddenly improve. Remember: development is not linear.

It's easy to forget our old opinions of Lawrence now that we have new opinions to form about Maye and Herbert. A year from now, we'll likely forget how we felt about Herbert and Maye in favor of a new C.J. Stroud or Jordan Love or Caleb Williams or Bryce Young or Tyler Shough take. There are so many young quarterbacks and so many conclusions to draw from such small samples.

Our eagerness to react to the next game limits our ability to see the forest for the trees. To see the totality of a quarterback beyond his most recent stat sheet. It's why I always chuckle when someone demands I admit that [insert quarterback here] is good/bad after his most recent game seemingly proves me wrong. Do you really want me to change my whole opinion on a player after just one game?

Herbert and Maye are far from the only quarterbacks with shaky early-season performances. Kyler Murray, Baker Mayfield ... even players such as Burrow and Matthew Stafford have been below form. Let's all take a collective breath and remember not to etch conclusions in September stone.

I think ... the Rams should make one more trade
Just one more trade, then we're done. Really.

Much like when I begged my mother for one more battle of Super Smash Bros. Melee on the GameCube when I was 9 (I mained Link), quarterback Matthew Stafford should be imploring GM Les Snead for one more trade. The defense had all the offseason fun, acquiring Trent McDuffie and Myles Garrett for the low cost of two first-round picks, a second-round pick, a third-round pick, a fifth-round pick, a sixth-round pick, a seventh-round pick and Jared Verse. When is the offense's turn?

Editor's note: Technically the Rams traded for receiver Tutu Atwell as well, but that's not really fun, is it?

Despite the fact that the Rams traded almost an entire year's worth of picks for two players, they're still in a position at which one more trade makes sense: specifically, for a pass catcher.

Los Angeles dressed five tight ends and four receivers Sunday in the absence of star receiver Puka Nacua and were treated with another turn-back-the-clock performance by Davante Adams: 7 catches for 137 yards. Combined with his 195 yards from the Rams' Week 2 "Monday Night Football" win, Adams has 332 receiving yards over the past two weeks -- the most he has ever had in a two-game span in his career.

Despite how cool it has been to see Adams reach unprecedented levels ... the Rams cannot live like this. Adams is a 33-year-old receiver who finished last season hobbled with a hamstring injury. Now he's seeing No. 1 receiver volume thanks in part to the lack of receiver depth behind him -- Jordan Whittington, Atwell and Xavier Smith were non-factors against the Broncos. The rise of Konata Mumpfield, who scored a touchdown Sunday night, is commendable but not something to be relied upon.

What's the big deal? Nacua will come back from his hip injury, surely -- the Rams are reportedly being cautious with him because of his importance to the offense. But now both Nacua and Adams require careful maintenance for their usage and health -- the dings they've recently suffered are unlikely to be the last. The rise of second-year tight end Terrance Ferguson, who was supposed to emerge as a quality third target ... is also impeded by an ankle injury of uncertain severity. He left, came back and left again against the Broncos in Week 3.

No team is well equipped to handle injuries to star players, but the Rams are particularly susceptible at receiver. They funnel targets to Nacua at league-leading rates and have now done so to Adams in his absence. The No. 3 receiver and lower spots on this team are reserved more for blocking and special teams value. Even adjusting for McVay's ability to scheme it up, a big injury after the trade deadline won't be easily backfilled with internal options.

So where to look? The Rams aren't the team that should kick the tires on a discontented first-round pick such as Marvin Harrison Jr. or Quentin Johnston -- they need a steady producer who can eat volume if needed. Chris Godwin Jr. might get out of Tampa Bay as the 0-3 Buccaneers pivot to younger players. Could Courtland Sutton be available from the Broncos, who are moving to a bigger diet of Jaylen Waddle and Pat Bryant? Do the Bills need both Joshua Palmer and Keon Coleman?

If this seems excessive, it should -- and that's good. The Rams are in for a penny, and the most obvious route to getting in for a pound -- if they're not already -- is by buttressing the depth at pass catcher. It's not the reason the Rams are 1-2 right now, but now that their margins for losing games is much smaller, it's a potential hot spot that must be addressed preventatively.

I think ... Steelers-Browns is suddenly a fun (and important) game
Don't look now, but the entire AFC North is 2-1! (Please ignore the fact that the Steelers and Browns have point differentials of minus-7 and minus-17, respectively.)

Independent of the records and the stakes, the Thursday night game between the Steelers and Browns in Cleveland has become an interesting one because of coaching changes to two units I thought might be entrenched in their particular approaches. Steelers coach Mike McCarthy and offensive coordinator Brian Angelichio have breathed fresh life into the Pittsburgh offense, and Browns defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg has given Cleveland's defense new layers of depth and complexity.

Let's start with the Steelers' offense, which in Week 3 did the one thing the Bengals were hoping would never happen again: It ran the ball on Cincinnati. Jaylen Warren had 69 rushing yards before contact in this game -- the biggest single-game number he has ever had. (That's with a sick 87-yard run wiped out by DK Metcalf's pretty inconsequential holding penalty, by the way.)

The Steelers' offensive line rose to the occasion against the Bengals' much improved front. With two new starters at right guard (Brock Hoffman) and right tackle (first-round pick Max Iheanachor), the Steelers felt comfortable running into the heart of the Bengals' defense, where Warren consistently made the Bengals' pair of inconsistent, young linebackers (Demetrius Knight Jr. and Barrett Carter) miss in tight areas.

Pittsburgh also used its deep room of tight ends to borrow some 49ers running concepts, pitching the ball out wide and getting lead blockers in motion while ignoring Bengals' Dexter Lawrence II on the interior entirely. With both the vertical and horizontal running games popping, quarterback Aaron Rodgers was able to get to a play-action game that created explosives -- the golden goose at this stage of his career, when it's harder for him to extend plays or make tight-window throws over the middle. Rodgers had the longest time to throw (3.19 seconds) that he has ever had as a Steeler, and 18.9% of his dropbacks were under-center play-action -- his highest since Week 3 of last season.

With an impactful running game and a functional play-action passing game, the Steelers have an offense that can run with a top-10 defense (I'm not sure they have that without Joey Porter Jr., but it's possible) and make some noise in the postseason. That offense is still a work in progress, and it will get a solid test against the Browns' defense in Week 4.

Perhaps the most dominant performance of Week 3 that went unremarked upon was the Browns' defense against the Panthers. After consecutive 30-point outings in which it looked like the Panthers could pass against just about anyone, they scored only three points in the first half -- on a drive the Browns' defense committed three penalties.

The Bengals' defensive tackle group is good at holding its ground and freeing up space for the linebackers. The Browns' group gets upfield. Rutenberg has retained that key feature of former coordinator Jim Schwartz's philosophy, and the Browns' talented group of young defensive linemen (Mason Graham, Jared Verse and Mike Hall Jr.) splashed disruption and created run stuffs against Carolina's usually effective running game.

But in the defensive backfield, Rutenberg has been more creative in his rotations and pressure packages. Some of the invention is needed to account for cornerback Tyson Campbell's injury -- the Browns started Mekhi Blackmon, who was claimed off waivers in August -- but it was also game-plan specific. The Browns dropped safeties into the low hole consistently at the snap, taking away Young's quick crossers and slants and forcing him into prolonged dropbacks in which Cleveland's pass rush won fast and often. Young was pressured on 40% of his dropbacks in this game, and you saw the Browns' seven QB hits accumulate over time.

The matchup between the Browns' defense and Steelers' offense is particularly interesting because of the impact star cornerback Denzel Ward can have. He blanketed Panthers receiver Tetairoa McMillan in Week 3 (26 matchups, 2 targets, 1 reception, 12 yards) and should have the same impact on Metcalf in Pittsburgh, which will force the ball to the Steelers' secondary pass catchers. For the 2025 Steelers, that was a terrible sign. But the Steelers had Roman Wilson, Ben Skowronek and Darnell Washington as key contributions in a spread-the-wealth win against Cincinnati on Sunday. Will the Browns have Campbell back to handle that? Can their speedy but undersized linebackers deal with physicality from the Steelers' Pat Freiermuth and Washington?

The Browns' penetrating front and willingness to blitz also presents a new challenge to the refurbished right side of the Steelers' line, for whom communication and chemistry must be tested. Steelers rookie right tackle Max Iheanachor going up against former Rams edge rusher Jared Verse is one of the best power-for-power matchups we'll see in this young season. Defensive tackle Mason Graham, the No. 5 pick in 2025, is having a breakout Year 2, but Steelers' Zach Frazier is an all-universe center through three games. And remember: Rutenberg was on the Jets' defensive staff from 2021 to 2024 and got an up-close look at what Rodgers can -- and can't -- do at this stage in his career.

My gut is leaning toward the Browns leading the AFC North this time next week. Weird times!

I think ... I'll never trust the Bills
I left the Bills off my very official postseason bracket prediction, and Buffalo fans have been roasting me on social media ever since. Fair play. The Bills are 3-0, and the Patriots (1-2) look like a mess in the division. Let's walk back to the top of the AFC East, where the Bills have long been and truly belong.

But it's exactly games such as Sunday's that make it so challenging to trust the Bills. The NFL season is a long and winding labyrinth to the Super Bowl, and around any corner lurks these disastrous offensive performances -- the Bills have stacked enough of them now that they cannot be ignored.

Against the Chargers (0-3), the Bills turned the ball over five times. Buffalo is the first team to win a game with 5-plus turnovers and a turnover margin of minus-4 or worse since the 2023 Jaguars, who beat the Chargers in the wild-card round of the playoffs. Before that, the last such team to win was the 2015 Denver Broncos in a Week 17 game against -- I'll give you one guess -- the San Diego Chargers.

Buffalo would have lost Sunday were it not for the Chargers' gross incompetence and apparent decades-long hex to lose such games. The Bills fumbled three times. One was a classic Josh Allen gaffe in the pocket in which he overestimated his own strength. Another was a concerning continuation of a trend for James Cook III, who -- as my colleague Bill Barnwell noted -- now has eight fumbles in his past 19 games.

Allen also threw two interceptions. One was a deep throw into double coverage -- he likely thought he had an offsides penalty given the early step from a Chargers defensive tackle, but he couldn't confirm the flag on the play-action fake and was punished for his heave. The other pick has no such excuses. Allen stares right into the heart of a quarters safety and tries to throw the ball so hard it passes through his material body.

In a vacuum, it would be unfair to freak out too much about this game. But Allen has these games. His last game with a minus-4 turnover margin was the divisional-round playoff loss to the Broncos. Easily remembered is his catastrophic fumble at the end of the first half to set up a Broncos field goal. It was joined by another fumble deep in his own territory to set up another field goal and a pick in Broncos territory to waste a short field. These were devastating plays in a game that went to overtime and was eventually lost on a second, controversial interception.

The Bills are capable of these high-turnover games against any quality of opponent -- last season, they lost 30-13 to a Dolphins team that was on a seven-game losing streak on the back of three giveaways. The Bills' offensive line now looks healthier than it did during that stretch last season, but still the Chargers' starting edge rusher duo of Khalil Mack and Tuli Tuipulotu had a combined 11 pressures and 2.5 sacks.

High-pressure teams bring out the wild side of Allen, who has grown admirably into a far more risk-averse quarterback than he once was. Still, the same big-play magic that makes the Bills seem unbeatable at times is also what makes the Bills eminently beatable -- by anyone -- when they catch some bad luck.

Buffalo got away with it this time. The Bills can even get away with it against superior opponents -- they have before, because Allen is that special. But this is the sort of game that puts the heebie-jeebies in me when I consider a potential postseason run.

I think ... J.J. McCarthy will save neither himself nor the Giants
But I'm still excited to watch him try!

The short but fraught tenure of McCarthy, the No. 10 pick of the 2024 draft, and the Vikings has ended, as the quarterback was traded to the Giants this week for a fifth-round pick. The Giants are looking for a serviceable bridge quarterback in Jaxson Dart's absence, and the Vikings were looking for ... well, just about any reason to move on from McCarthy.

It's important to recall just how bad McCarthy's 2025 season was. Since 2010, there have been 541 seasons played by a quarterback with at least 250 dropbacks. McCarthy's 2025 QBR (36.1) ranks 498th, his interception per dropback (4.2%) ranks 531st and his sack per dropback (9.4%) ranks 509th.

That interception/sack rate -- 13.6% all together -- is a walloping number. Almost one out of every seven dropbacks from McCarthy last season ended in a sack or a pick. It does not matter how good the throws are when you actually connect on them. There is no path to quarterbacking relevancy that bypasses those two numbers. McCarthy cuts a dramatic number of his interceptions and sacks, or he isn't viable. Simple as that.

Is there historical precedent for such an evolution? Giants fans should know the answer to that. Eli Manning had worse interception performances in the 2010 (25 picks, 4.4% rate) and 2013 (27 picks, 4.5% rate) seasons. In between, he made two Pro Bowls.

The issue, of course, is that Manning had a low sack rate when he was throwing all those picks. It's the combination that kills you. In 2013, Geno Smith (Jets) had a combined number of 12.4%, and it took him several seasons of bouncing around as a backup to find resurrection. Other significant names with big interception and sack rates include 2022 Justin Fields (15.0%, oh my heavens), 2024 Will Levis (14.6%), 2011 Christian Ponder (12.6%), 2021 Zach Wilson (12.4%). Does anybody feel good?

Smith is evidence that a high ranking on the list is not a death knell, and there's more to join him. Ryan Tannehill in 2018 was at 14.0%, then went on to be a perfectly acceptable quarterback for the Titans. Lamar Jackson was at 11.7% just last season after an MVP year!

The thing is, you have to pay off your negatives with big positives, and while McCarthy had an acceptable rate of explosive passes last season ... it wasn't nearly enough. That was in an offense built around explosive plays over anything else: long dropbacks, deep-developing routes, under-center play-action fakes. In New York, McCarthy will get more spread looks and RPOs from the gun. Does he have the poise, field vision and accuracy to create explosive plays in that passing game?

I'm dubious ... but I am interested. The offensive line in New York is far better than the banged-up line the Vikings had for McCarthy in 2025. McCarthy is a slippery mover who should be involved in the option running game, though he needs to protect himself from hits, as he has collected far too many knocks over his short time in the league. I can see Matt Nagy and Greg Roman, the two primary offensive designers in New York, coming up with good, risk-averse game plans that dramatically lower McCarthy's time to throw (3.22 seconds last season, 14th longest for a QB since 2010) and minimize his opportunities for post-snap decisions.

Is that enough to keep the Giants' season afloat? I doubt it. I love the running game talent, but the lack of depth at pass catcher will hurt them against teams that can take away receiver Malik Nabers with either scheme or personnel. I love the pass rush but worry that big-boy offenses will run all over them. The Giants are an incomplete team -- a totally acceptable thing to be, in Year 1 of the John Harbaugh era -- and incomplete teams lack the internal structure to support imperfect quarterbacks such as McCarthy.

Quarterback reclamation, while more common in recent years, is a finicky process. It has mostly happened in the Sean McVay/Kyle Shanahan systems (that's not what New York runs), and it usually happens after a couple of years in the family, too. McCarthy is a midseason acquisition away from that coaching tree. Getting out of Minnesota and turning his career to a fresh page was the first step on a long path to return to relevancy. I'm not ruling it out -- it's a crazy league -- but I'm not holding my breath for it. It'll take longer than my lungs have capacity for.

Five things I might think

I might think ... we haven't seen the Kyler Murray offense yet. In Murray's first full game as Vikings quarterback, Minnesota had the worst offensive success rate it has had in a game under Kevin O'Connell. Some of that has to do with the style the Vikings are running with Murray (he was hunting deep passes all game). But still, there are a lot of bad backup QBs in that sample -- spooky stuff.

I'm not too worried there. The Vikings' No. 1 receiver (Justin Jefferson, you might have heard of him) went down early because of an ankle injury in Week 3 (but avoided serious injury), which is obviously a big deal. No. 1 running back Jordan Mason (thumb) is also still on injured reserve. This is a very new offense to Murray, and it's going to take time to acclimate before we even consider the absences. No panic button for me yet.

I might think ... the Bears have a QB controversy. Just kidding. But how about the veteran pulling out a 27-7 win over the Eagles! No. 3 QB Case Keenum did his job as the quick-distribution point guard in Ben Johnson's suddenly quick and spread-out offense. The Bears absolutely got the drop on the Eagles with a different approach than Johnson's offense has typically used, and they might not get such a surprise factor in future games. But their next three opponents are the Jets, Packers and Falcons (who have combined for a total of three wins) -- and Keenum likely won't be the quarterback for all three, as No. 2 Tyson Bagent returns from concussion protocol.

I'm impressed by the way Johnson changed the offense to account for the lack of Caleb Williams (hamstring), and I'm confident he can do it week over week to keep the Bears afloat until their star passer returns.

I might think ... the Dolphins are being punished for something. The lone known commodity among all Dolphins skill position players was running back De'Von Achane, whom they could have traded but valued so much they kept him. Now he is lost for the season to a torn ACL in his left knee. The Dolphins' three opponents so far (Raiders, 49ers and Chiefs) are a combined 9-0 ... and their Week 4 opponent is the 3-0 Vikings.

I might think ... the Ravens have a Marlon Humphrey problem. It was a nice last-second win there for the Ravens, but the target the Cowboys put on Humphrey in coverage was ... concerning. On 37 coverage snaps, the cornerback saw 10 targets and surrendered 6 catches for 108 yards and a score -- the Cowboys were especially attacking him on late downs and in the red zone. I'm monitoring the Ravens for cornerback trades as we transition into the fall.

I might think ... defensive pass interference will be reviewable by this time next year. There were two game-changing calls in Cowboys-Ravens and Rams-Broncos. Only one actually flipped the outcome (bad luck, Rams fans) -- but it was in primetime for a Super Bowl favorite. A few more of those, and we're going to see the ever-expanding reach of replay assist extend into pass interference calls. So long as it's the speedy assist method, and not the prolonged review method, I'm all for it. There's nothing I respect less than receivers farming pass interference instead of playing the ball.

stories.headline: 2026 MLB playoffs: Our predictions for every round
stories.summary: Who will be the last one standing in October? Our MLB experts predict which team will win each series of the postseason.
stories.body:
The 2026 MLB playoffs kick off Tuesday afternoon with 12 teams vying for the chance to hoist this year's World Series trophy.

The Dodgers look to further cement their dynasty by becoming the first National League team to three-peat as World Series champions, while the Brewers hope to win their first title in club history coming off a franchise-record 103-win regular season. And don't forget about the Rays and Guardians, who also hold first-round byes and hope to make it far in October. After securing a postseason berth on the final day of the season, the Phillies seek to capitalize on their contention window to win their first title since 2008 -- and they join the rest of the wild-card teams, including the Yankees and Red Sox, in their quest to shake up the playoffs and make deep runs.

Who will win each round? And which squad will be the last standing at the end of the postseason? We asked 24 of our MLB experts -- from ESPN Digital, TV, Research and more -- to give us their predictions.

Below are their picks for the wild-card winners, division series winners, championship series winners and, ultimately, the World Series champion.

Everything you need to know | Bracket

American League Wild Card Series

ALWC: Chicago White Sox vs. Houston Astros

Chicago White Sox, 13 votes

Houston Astros, 11 votes

Our voters were split pretty evenly between Chicago and Houston. Why are the White Sox your pick? Both these teams have some deficiencies as compared with other playoff powerhouses. But the White Sox have strengths that should matter in October: left-handed sluggers and a bullpen. In a short series, manager Will Venable will deploy his pen early and often -- though the impact of that could be felt in the next round if Chicago advances. On offense, Munetaka Murakami is in better rhythm now than he was for most of the season's second half. Combined with Miguel Vargas, it gives the White Sox some nice balance. If they can contain Houston's Yordan Alvarez -- and that's a big if -- they should win the series in three games. -- Jesse Rogers

And why are the Astros yours? Are the Astros a good team? No. But they have the best hitter on the planet in 2026 in Alvarez. They led the majors in home runs. They have a lights-out closer in Josh Hader. They don't have much pitching depth, which is why they finished .500, but that's not a big factor in a three-game series. And it's not as if Chicago is exactly running out Greg Maddux, Tom Glavine and John Smoltz in its rotation. The White Sox have power, as well, but they strike out a ton; and over each of the past three months, they hit .225, .232 and .228, respectively. -- David Schoenfield

ALWC: Boston Red Sox vs. New York Yankees

New York Yankees 18

Boston Red Sox 6

After a historic run in July and August catapulted them into playoff contention, the Red Sox went .500 in September to finish out the season. What needs to happen for them to beat the Yankees in New York? The Red Sox might not have the best pitcher in this series, but they have multiple left-handers to throw at a team susceptible to them and also have a stronger bullpen depth. Boston's lefties -- a group that could include the recovering Garrett Crochet, though his status is "up in the air" for the wild-card series, according to manager Chad Tracy -- could prove to be problematic for sluggers Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger, among other Yankees.

What if Aaron Judge plays for New York? Well, what if he does? He was a minor factor in September, when he rushed back from a rib injury only to suffer a right calf strain and land back on the injured list. Neither team has had a potent offense lately, not like when they met last October, but I like Boston's pitching in this year's matchup. -- Eric Karabell

National League Wild Card Series

NLWC: Philadelphia Phillies vs. Atlanta Braves

Atlanta Braves 18

Philadelphia Phillies 6

The Phillies struggled down the stretch. How do they rebound to beat the Braves? If Philadelphia's down-the-stretch struggles were predictive of postseason doom, sportsbooks wouldn't price them as nearly a coin flip to beat Atlanta (+105 at DraftKings as of this writing). Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski's stars-and-scrubs roster is likely to falter in a longer series, but in the short term, his quintet of Cristopher Sanchez, Zack Wheeler, Jhoan Duran, Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber will carry Philadelphia past its longtime division rival, again. -- Paul Hembekides

Tell us why you think Atlanta comes out on top: The Phillies have a big advantage as a team in their rotation, but they'll have little-to-no advantage on the day they face Atlanta's Chris Sale -- Game 1 of the three-game wild-card series. The bullpens are of similar quality, and the lineups are also similar -- I give the Braves slight edges in both spots. This season, there has been a 36-run gap (i.e. roughly 3½ wins over the regular season) in their defensive performance, which helps explain why the Braves' pitchers outperformed their ERA estimators by about half a run while the Phillies were a bit worse than theirs. The Braves can hit homers, catch the ball and lean on the bullpen -- and Sale -- to a narrow victory in three games. -- Kiley McDaniel

NLWC: Chicago Cubs vs. San Diego Padres

San Diego Padres 17

Chicago Cubs 7

San Diego has momentum on its side, as Chicago fizzled a bit toward season's end. What would the Cubs need to do to knock out the Padres? Anyone facing the Padres needs to play with a lead because Craig Stammen can start rolling out a bullpen map that leads to Mason Miller by the fourth or fifth inning, if the San Diego manager needs to. That makes getting to San Diego's starters during the first trip through the order crucial. The Cubs have the offense to do that and the defense to keep San Diego off the board, provided their pitchers can keep the Pads in the park. -- Bradford Doolittle

American League Division Series

ALDS: Winner of White Sox-Astros vs. Cleveland Guardians

Cleveland Guardians 19

Houston Astros 3

Chicago White Sox 2

The Guardians enter October with momentum and as a favorite to advance to the AL Championship Series. Why is that? The first-round bye plays into Cleveland's strengths: It can line up its starting pitching and properly rest a bullpen that was used heavily as the Guardians pushed for a playoff spot -- and their eventual AL Central division title -- down the stretch. They go into the playoffs as the league's hottest team, winning 24 of their final 35 games -- second to only Milwaukee over that span. Their offense has been more productive of late, with Steven Kwan, Travis Bazzana and, most importantly, Jose Ramirez finishing strong. Ramirez, who missed five weeks following left hand surgery in mid-June, seems to be gaining strength in his wrist as the season goes on. They're all heating up at the right time. -- Buster Olney

ALDS: Winner of Red Sox-Yankees vs. Tampa Bay Rays

Tampa Bay Rays 18

New York Yankees 4

Boston Red Sox 2

You were part of the majority that chose the Rays. What makes them your pick? The Rays are 55-26 at Tropicana Field this year, and they have home-field advantage in the division series. But they're a challenge wherever they play, because they play a different game than any other team in the league. They bunt way more than any other team, they put the ball in play when Junior Caminero isn't putting it in the outfield seats and they run the bases until you tag them out. Plus, they can really pitch. Tampa Bay pitchers walked 409 batters, by far the fewest in baseball. The Rays throw strikes, they swing at strikes and they play the game correctly. That's enough to get the them to the ALCS. -- Tim Kurkjian

National League Division Series

NLDS: Winner of Phillies-Braves vs. Los Angeles Dodgers

Los Angeles Dodgers 23

Atlanta Braves 1

The Dodgers were an almost unanimous pick to advance out of the division series. Why are they seen as such a lock? It's very simple: Whoever faces them will have to get through Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and, if necessary, Tyler Glasnow. No team can match the potential dominance of that group from top to bottom. The Dodgers are not perfect, of course. There are questions going in about the health of Shohei Ohtani, the production of Kyle Tucker and the reliability of Edwin Diaz, among other issues. But at the end of the day, the Dodgers will roll out essentially four aces. That's tough to beat. -- Alden Gonzalez

NLDS: Winner of Cubs-Padres vs. Milwaukee Brewers

Milwaukee Brewers 22

San Diego Padres 2

You were one of just two voters to pick the Padres over the Brewers. Why do you think that San Diego can pull off the upset? The Brewers were tied for the second-best record in the majors with the Rays after July 23. The only team better? The Padres. San Diego went 41-18 during a stretch that coincided with the offense flipping from one of the worst in baseball to one of the best behind Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill. The Padres' starting rotation is concerning, but they have a top-tier bullpen built for October with Mason Miller looming in the ninth inning and October-tested stars in the lineup. Two years ago, they nearly knocked off the Dodgers, the NL's No. 1 seed, in the NLDS. This year, they get it done against top-seeded Milwaukee. -- Jorge Castillo

American League Championship Series

Tampa Bay Rays 18

New York Yankees 4

Boston Red Sox 2

Tampa Bay holds only a one-game lead over the Yankees in head-to-head competition in 2026, but the Rays are our voters' overwhelming favorite to win the pennant. Why will New York come out on top? It's the Yankees' pitching, which presents them with a greater advantage than any postseason team New York has had in quite a while. The team ERA is the Yankees' best since 1978, and their ERA+ (130) is their second-best mark ever, thanks to a stout four-man rotation of Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon (the latter of whom might not even be needed for a five-game division series).

New York's toughest matchups come in the first two rounds -- versus the 87-win Red Sox and the 1-seed Rays -- but those short series give the Yankees the luxury of mixing and matching their pitching, which is something they haven't been quite as able to do in recent years. This year, I see the Yankees being tough to beat in the tighter, more pitching-oriented games of October. -- Tristan Cockcroft

National League Championship Series
Milwaukee Brewers 16

Los Angeles Dodgers 7

San Diego Padres 1

In last year's NLCS, the Dodgers swept the top-seeded Brewers. A majority of our voters, including you, have Milwaukee advancing this time around. Explain your reasoning. This is a significantly better Brewers team than last year's -- and one more equipped to handle the Dodgers' starting-pitching gauntlet. Jackson Chourio is better. Brice Turang is better. Garrett Mitchell is better. Jake Bauers is way better. And while the offense does matter (remember, the Brewers hit .118/.191/.193 in the NLCS last year), Milwaukee's pitching is improved too.

Between Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson, the Brewers boast two of the toughest-to-hit starters in baseball. And the bullpen, a strength in 2025, is every bit as good this year and might actually get some leads to hold onto. Yes, the Dodgers finished seven games ahead of where they were in 2025, so it's not like they're flailing, particularly with how strongly they wrapped up the regular season. The Brewers are simply surging more; now is their time. -- Jeff Passan

World Series

Milwaukee Brewers 14

(Buster Olney, Tim Kurkjian, David Schoenfield, Brendan DeAngelis, Jeff Passan, Dan Mullen, AJ Mass, Jesse Rogers, Tim Keown, Tristan Cockcroft, Eric Karabell, JJ Post, Kiley McDaniel, Bradford Doolittle)

Los Angeles Dodgers 6

(Sean Coyle, Jorge Castillo, Jacob Nitzberg, Gregg Colli, Matt Marrone, Liz Finny)

Tampa Bay Rays 4

(Paul Hembekides, Scott Gustafson, Alden Gonzalez, Doug Glanville)

The Brewers were our most popular pick, even though they've faltered the past few postseasons they've played in. Why is this year different? The Brewers are the most well-rounded team in the majors -- pitching, offense, defense, speed, manager. They play hard and execute small ball when needed, and this is a better team than previous editions. The Brewers obviously have an ace in Misiorowski, but they also have the most underrated No. 2 starter in baseball in Henderson. Critics point to Milwaukee's lack of power -- after finishing tied for 28th in home runs -- but the team was second in the majors in runs, and Chourio (.917 OPS over the final two months), Bauers (third in the majors in OBP) and Turang (61 extra-base hits, 100 RBIs) can do enough damage in the middle of the lineup. -- Schoenfield

Los Angeles was the favorite in our preseason predictions to win the World Series. Now, entering October, only six voters out of 24 picked the Dodgers. What makes you think they'll secure the three-peat? I picked against the Dodgers the last two years, so I've decided I'm not going to do that again. Yes, they have the oldest roster in the majors, and it has shown throughout the season. Yes, Ohtani and others are banged up. Yes, the bullpen has questions and the offense was inconsistent all year. People around the sport put those facts together and say they believe they're vulnerable. And yet the Dodgers won 100 games to run away with another NL West title. They're still the most talented team in baseball with stars everywhere. I've learned my lesson: Don't pick against the Dodgers. -- Castillo

Most of our voters had an NL team raising the trophy, but you were one of four to pick Tampa Bay. How can the Rays come out victorious in the Fall Classic? There are many great NL clubs this season, but only one team wins the trophy -- and the Rays are every bit as good as the best teams out there. When asking a range of players, managers and announcers which teams were the toughest they played this year, the Rays always come up.

The theme I hear a lot is that the Rays have a nightmare lineup, especially at the top: In the 3- or 4-spot you have Caminero, a game-changing power hitter, and the rest of the order is the definition of contact, chameleons and havoc. No easy outs, and they present challenges in different ways. Hard to defend. Like always, they pitch well and catch the ball -- but any year the Rays get offense, like this one, watch out. And let's not forget, manager Kevin Cash has been doing this forever. He is smart, prepared and knows his team and organization as well as anyone knows theirs. So, why not the Rays? -- Glanville

stories.headline: NBA 2026-27 preseason: Answering big questions for all 30 teams
stories.summary: From LeBron James' fit in Philadelphia to Kawhi Leonard's return to Toronto, we're answering the biggest preseason questions for all 30 teams.
stories.body:
Monday's media day kicked off NBA training camps around the league and offered a first look at several stars in their new homes. The Philadelphia 76ers had perhaps the biggest offseason, adding Jaylen Brown on July 1 and then the league's all-time leading scorer LeBron James before the month was over. But the Sixers aren't the only ones who made big moves.

James' former team, the Los Angeles Lakers, took a big swing in trading for former Jazz center Walker Kessler, and Giannis Antetokounmpo finally found a new home in the Miami Heat. LaMelo Ball is teaming up with Anthony Edwards and the Minnesota Timberwolves, and Ja Morant will look for a fresh start with the Portland Trail Blazers.

Big trades and signings aren't the only noteworthy storylines coming out of the offseason. Will the Detroit Pistons resolve Jalen Duren's contract dispute? How will the San Antonio Spurs rebound after collapsing in the Finals? Our NBA Insiders answer the biggest preseason questions for all 30 teams.

Jump to a team:

ATL | BOS | BKN | CHA | CHI | CLE

DAL | DEN | DET | GS | HOU | IND

LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN

NO | NY | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX

POR | SAC | SA | TOR | UTAH | WAS

Atlanta Hawks
Will the Hawks build on their strong finish to last season?

To be clear, the Hawks' 51-point loss in their elimination game isn't the strong finish we are referring to. But Atlanta did account for two of the Knicks' three playoff losses, and the Hawks went on a 19-4 run with a plus-13.9 average point differential at the end of the regular season after committing to CJ McCollum in the starting lineup.

Atlanta added to the roster this summer -- drafting Kingston Flemings in the lottery and trading for ring-earning role players Lu Dort and Aaron Wiggins -- and is positioned to be aggressive at the trade deadline or next summer, when the Hawks could have about $45 million in salary cap space. -- Tim MacMahon

Boston Celtics
Is Jayson Tatum ready to assume command of the Celtics on the court?

Tatum made it a point to get back on the court before last season ended, proving his Achilles injury couldn't keep him down. The results were mixed in the short term, as his regular-season percentages were down across the board and he sat out Game 7 of the Celtics' first-round series because of left knee discomfort.

Trading Jaylen Brown was a full endorsement of Tatum's ability to take the throttle while retooling to get back to championship status. But is Tatum fully recovered from the injury and ready to assume control? -- Vincent Goodwill

Brooklyn Nets
Can the Nets go from deplorable to dependable?

The Nets invested in a long-term rebuilding plan: think of those first-round picks Sean Marks held onto in the 2025 draft, rather than attempting to aggregate them for impact players. But then lottery reform happened, forcing the Nets to press the fast-forward button in July.

Trading for Julius Randle upgraded their talent, as did drafting another point guard in Mikel Brown Jr. Can this team look competent without the benefit of knowing another high draft pick is on the way? -- Goodwill

Charlotte Hornets
Can the Hornets be a better team after trading two cornerstone starters?

Charlotte has been very methodical in its build, and ownership and the front office have taken strides to avoid falling into the traps that ascending teams can sometimes make when they chase the middle. The Hornets got to the middle last season but clearly the team didn't believe that LaMelo Ball and Miles Bridges, both of whom have expensive contracts and will be searching for extensions soon, were part of the rise so they tried to maximize their position by trading both.

The acquisitions of veterans Naz Reid, Grayson Allen and Dennis Schroder, in theory, augment newly established cornerstones Brandon Miller and Kon Knueppel. But Charlotte needs to get Miller into an extension that makes sense for both sides -- an age-old tale -- and Knueppel suffered a moderate hamstring injury that is going to cause him to sit out all of training camp and the start of the season. In a very competitive Eastern Conference, getting back to the play-in might be a chore. -- Brian Windhorst

Chicago Bulls
Was summer league a preview of what we will see from Caleb Wilson?

No rookie had the Las Vegas gym buzzing quite like Wilson did this summer. He put up 35 points in his first game as a pro, knocked down as many 3-pointers in one game as his entire freshman season at North Carolina and rounded out his highlight reel with ferocious dunks and a chase-down block. For the first time in years, Wilson gives the Bulls a clear reason for optimism going forward. -- Jamal Collier

Cleveland Cavaliers
Can Peyton Watson make a difference as the fifth starter?

The Cavs have been heavily invested in four of their five starters for years -- Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen in the front court with Donovan Mitchell and now James Harden, after a midseason exchange for Darius Garland, in the backcourt. But they've had a rotating cast filling out the last spot next to them -- Dean Wade, Max Strus or De'Andre Hunter, most recently -- all of whom have failed to raise the ceiling of the lineup.

Watson, 24, is coming off his best season with the Nuggets and has the potential to push this group over the edge even more if he can continue his improved 3-point shooting to go along with his defensive chops. -- Collier

Dallas Mavericks
How much better can Cooper Flagg be as a sophomore?

Flagg is literally and figuratively growing up before our eyes. He got taller over the summer after his Rookie of the Year season, measuring at 6-foot-10 without his shoes. The fact that the 19-year-old Flagg is still growing serves as symbolism of his seemingly limitless ceiling. Fair or not, Flagg will always be compared in Dallas to Luka Doncic, who was a first-team All-NBA selection in his second season. Conventional wisdom is that Flagg is on the trajectory to ascend to that level of stardom. How soon can he get there? -- MacMahon

Denver Nuggets
Can Aaron Gordon stay healthy?

In his six seasons with the Nuggets, Gordon has only improved as a player and elevated as a fit next to Nikola Jokic. His importance has never been greater, but his availability has never been more in question. Gordon sat out 31 games two seasons ago and 46 games last season. Both playoff runs also ended with a hobbled Gordon dealing with a hamstring strain and a calf strain that either had him significantly limited or sidelined.

Denver's depth has eroded around Jokic, but when Gordon is healthy and productive on the wing, they still have as complete and feared of a five-man starting unit as any team. But how often will he be out there? Word is he is geared and ready for camp. -- Anthony Slater

Detroit Pistons
Will Jalen Duren attend training camp, and if so, how long will it take for him to acclimate?

The Duren saga has loomed over the Pistons all summer, and there still is no resolution. Duren was not at Pistons media day Monday and is not expected at the start of training camp, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. If Duren goes the extreme route of taking a qualifying offer, it won't make for a comfortable situation -- along with the unprecedented act of turning down $200 million.

Team chemistry and continuity were reasons Detroit went from 44 wins in 2024-25 to 60 last season, and the roster has gone through changes this offseason. The possibility of an unhappy Duren creates the possibility of a slow start in a stacked East. -- Goodwill

Golden State Warriors
When will we see Jimmy Butler?

Butler tore his right ACL on Jan. 19 and had surgery in early February. The early months of rehab went slow, but there was steady word over the summer from those around Butler that his knee was strengthening, his court work was increasing and the optimism about his ultimate recovery was growing. Butler told ESPN in June he expected to get back "to who I've always been."

He will be limited to individual court work when camp opens. A January or February timeline appears to be a soft target, but it will depend on how his knee responds to increased contact once he is cleared. The Warriors' viability as a dark horse playoff threat is almost entirely contingent on Butler getting back to somewhere near his old self before April. -- Slater

Houston Rockets
Will the Rockets finally advance beyond the first round of the playoffs?

Houston hasn't advanced past the opening round since the 2019-20 season and is coming off back-to-back first-round exits as future Hall of Famer Kevin Durant enters his second season as a Rocket. Season-ending injuries to veterans Fred VanVleet and Steven Adams created somewhat of a gap year for Houston in 2025-26.

But at the same time, several young players such as Amen Thompson, Reed Sheppard, Tari Eason, Alperen Sengun and Jabari Smith Jr. grew due to increased responsibilities created by the loss of the team's main offensive facilitator. Will that development carry over to this season for a team that fancies itself a contender? Is VanVleet truly the missing ingredient? We'll see. -- Michael C. Wright

Indiana Pacers
What can the Pacers expect from Tyrese Haliburton?

It has been 16 months since Haliburton's most recent game when the Pacers put together one of the most memorable playoff runs in league history as he went on an all-time run of clutch performances. How well Haliburton will bounce back from his Achilles injury is a perplexing wrinkle in an Eastern Conference that has become even more competitive since he last played. Can Haliburton reclaim his spot at the top of the contenders or has the rest of the competition passed him by? -- Collier

LA Clippers
What will be the fallout from the league's punishment for the Kawhi Leonard saga?

Leonard is now in Toronto, but it's not as if it was a clean break after seven seasons with the franchise. Clippers owner Steve Ballmer is suspended for a year, as is president of business operations Gillian Zucker. President of basketball operations, Lawrence Frank, is suspended six months. The franchise was fined $30 million and will be docked five first-round draft picks between now and 2033.

With all that swirling around, how will this new-look roster with the likes of Brandon Ingram, Darius Garland, Bradley Beal, Rui Hachimura, Max Strus and Brook Lopez -- alongside rookie Keaton Wagler -- be able to compete in an unforgiving Western Conference? -- Dave McMenamin

Los Angeles Lakers
Will the bet on Walker Kessler pay off?

The Lakers pushed virtually all of their chips to the middle of the table to make a move on the 25-year-old and pair the 7-2 center alongside Luka Doncic's wizardry. The cost was prohibitive: not just a four-year, $130 million contract, but two unprotected future first-round picks and two future pick swaps sent to the Utah Jazz to make it happen. Lakers coach JJ Redick called Kessler a "perfect fit" alongside Doncic and Austin Reaves before training camp even opened, and L.A.'s president of basketball operations and general manager, Rob Pelinka, defended the gamble by suggesting that it was the only viable way to land a player like Kessler.

"There's a scarcity of supply," Pelinka said. "There just is. And if you look at what you could potentially get in the draft or what is potentially going to come in free agency, those centers just don't exist."

If Kessler is everything L.A. hopes he will be, it will all be worth it. If he's not, the franchise will be in a tough spot with roster flexibility. -- McMenamin

Memphis Grizzlies
How soon can Memphis return to relevancy?

Grizzlies general manager Zach Kleiman confidently said last season at the trade deadline that fans shouldn't expect a long rebuild. And that was before Memphis traded franchise star Ja Morant to Portland. "We're not starting from scratch," Kleiman said. "We already have a lot to work with. I don't think this is some five-year, try to be terrible [by tanking process]."

The current roster features plenty of young talent in Zach Edey, Cedric Coward and No. 3 pick Cameron Boozer, but it appears the Grizzlies might still be a couple of years away from returning to the postseason. -- Wright

Miami Heat
How will Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo fit offensively?

After years of trying to add a superstar, the Heat finally traded for Antetokounmpo this summer. Together, he and Adebayo will be one of the most formidable front courts in the conference, but their fit offensively is much less clear.

Both have similar skill sets, play around the basket without much of an outside shooting game -- and both would be enchanted by a point guard helping create easy offense. The Heat are going to need a much healthier Antetokounmpo this season to compete in a crowded East and provide enough time to find offensive chemistry with Adebayo. -- Collier

Milwaukee Bucks
Do any of these players fit together?

There are no shortage of questions for how Milwaukee moves forward in the post-Giannis era, but in the aftermath of trading a franchise player, the Bucks' roster will be deeper than it was last season. But with so many capable rotation players, including a mix of veterans and young players, the onus will be on new coach Taylor Jenkins to figure out how all the players fit together on a nightly basis. The Bucks do not own their draft pick this season, which gives them incentives to try to remain competitive if they can find the right player combo. -- Collier

Minnesota Timberwolves
How quickly can LaMelo Ball and Anthony Edwards find the correct offensive balance?

The four-team blockbuster that landed Ball in Minnesota was finalized in early July. Ball has spent a chunk of the past two months in the team's practice facility in downtown Minneapolis getting acclimated with his new franchise and his new teammates. That has included Edwards, who has been around plenty the past month, attempting to expedite the progression for the league's most spectacular new backcourt experiment.

It will be a high bar for the Timberwolves to rise into the San Antonio and Oklahoma City tier, but if Ball and Edwards can figure out how to fuse and amplify each other's talents, they have the greatest chance among West competitors. -- Slater

New Orleans Pelicans
Did the Pelicans make a mistake in choosing to run it back with essentially the same group as last season?

It might look that way on the surface. But considering the immense talent on the roster -- from Dejounte Murray and Trey Murphy to Jeremiah Fears, Zion Williamson and Derik Queen -- it's clear that Joe Dumars and Troy Weaver believed the club's biggest offseason acquisition needed to be a coach to lead and cultivate all the talent.

Perhaps New Orleans found that in Jamahl Mosley, who presided over a rebuild in Orlando, leading the Magic to three consecutive postseason berths. The talented Williamson will always be a question because of his injury history. But don't be surprised to see the big man showcase a more consistent jumper this season. -- Wright

New York Knicks
Will Karl-Anthony Towns' contract extension standstill affect the champions' harmony?

The vibes were great for the Knicks all spring, culminating in a romp through the playoffs and their first championship in 53 years. Towns, the first of several Knicks impact players hoping to get extended, hasn't been rewarded with an offer he likes, as owner James Dolan issued the edict to avoid the punitive second apron.

If last season was one of sacrifice, will he fight the temptation to set himself up as a factor in a robust free agent market next summer? The Knicks will have the target on their backs all season long, and they can't afford to be disjointed in any way. -- Goodwill

Oklahoma City Thunder
Can Jalen Williams stay healthy?

Maybe the Thunder would have been the first repeat champions since the 2017-18 Warriors if not for Williams' recurring hamstring injuries that sidelined him for much of the regular season and the vast majority of the playoffs. The hope is that Oklahoma City won't have to wonder after a summer of Williams working on his body to maximize his chances of staying healthy.

Williams is one of the best two-way wings in the league when he's on the court -- a versatile, disruptive defender who also alleviates a lot of pressure on back-to-back MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander as a secondary creator. -- MacMahon

Orlando Magic
What will define this season: The Sweeney effect or a big trade?

Last season was a setback for the Magic, who invested heavily into their core of Paolo Banchero, Franz Wagner, Jalen Suggs and Desmond Bane. But, partially because of injuries, they backslid last season. The front office contemplated major moves last season and into the summer -- this is tough to believe, admittedly, because Jeff Weltman has been known for not making trades during his tenure -- but it did happen, per sources. Instead they decided to change the coach, firing the popular Jahmal Mosely and replacing him with Sean Sweeney, regarded as one of the top assistants in the league.

The Magic haven't been able to score when it truly matters and Banchero, to whom they've given a max contract, has not consistently been able to be part of effective lineups around the team's other cornerstones. So it's on Sweeney to see if tactical changes can make a difference. Sweeney has played a big role in helping the Mavericks and the Spurs get more out of their rosters over the past few seasons. If they don't, you might see the Magic in the rare position of being involved in trade rumors by midseason. -- Windhorst

Philadelphia 76ers
How long will it take for all the new players to come together?

As if trading for 2024 Finals MVP Jaylen Brown wasn't a dramatic enough fork in the road for the Sixers to navigate, four-time Finals MVP, four-time MVP and the league's all-time leading scorer, LeBron James, joined a few weeks later. There's no roadmap for coach Nick Nurse to follow to maximize a group like this, with not only those two new faces, but an ascendent star in Tyrese Maxey and the player who has been "the man" in Philadelphia for the past decade in Joel Embiid.

James, having played more NBA games than anyone in history, has seen it all and is anticipating the discovery period ahead. "We have to have a bunker mentality," James said on an episode of his podcast, "Mind the Game," last week. "The only thing that matters is what we preach every day and how we're going to hold each other accountable."

James has the experience to know to stay the course, but many of his new teammates haven't lived anywhere close to the same NBA existence that he has. -- McMenamin

Phoenix Suns
How does Jalen Green fit in with this group?

Phoenix was one of the surprise success stories in the league last season, winning 45 games in Jordan Ott's first year as a head coach and quickly pivoting from the lackluster Kevin Durant era. But most of that winning was done with 24-year-old shooting guard Green in street clothes. Green sat out 50 games because of persistent hamstring issues and in the games he did play, Phoenix went just 17-15. Initially seen as the key player in the Durant trade with the Rockets, it was Dillon Brooks who ended up having a breakout offensive season for the Suns while injuries limited Green.

Green's absence also allowed more minutes for Collin Gillespie and Jordan Goodwin, who both had strong seasons and were rewarded with new contracts in the offseason. Green is in the last year of his deal for $36.3 million, although he has a player option for next season at $36 million. Will he be able to find his stride if he can stay healthy, or will his best skill as a scorer be redundant with Devin Booker already filling that role as the leader of the team? -- McMenamin

Portland Trail Blazers
How do the Blazers fit all their guards?

The Blazers made Micah Nori the lowest-paid, shortest-term coach this summer and then gave him a mismatched roster in the middle of a storm about the future of the franchise. If you want to be an optimist, and why shouldn't one, Nori will probably get universal praise if he's able to stitch it together for even a middle-of-the-road season.

Damian Lillard is back, both in Portland and from an Achilles tear. That's awesome. Ja Morant has been acquired by trade after playing 79 games total the past three seasons. That's interesting. Jrue Holiday, two-time winner of the Joe Dumars NBA Sportsmanship Award and winner of the Kareem Abdul-Jabbar Social Justice Champion Award, is a rock of leadership. That's wonderful. Former No. 3 pick Scoot Henderson is coming off his best season, but is still trying to improve his efficiency and get a big contract extension this fall. That's something. Shaedon Sharpe is coming off his best season and is at the start of a four-year, $90 million contract but tore his meniscus and is expected to sit out most of the season. That's a bummer.

Figuring out how to make all of that work is going to be a huge key to the season. -- Windhorst

Sacramento Kings
Can Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis recharge their careers?

Both LaVine and Sabonis have been available for trade during the past few transition cycles, but Kings general manager Scott Perry has not received an appealing enough offer to strike. So both veterans return to a young team in transition, serving essentially as starting placeholders without much obvious loyalty to the franchise's future.

It would benefit both sides if they play well. Internally, the Kings are intent on making at least a small leap from the 22 games they won last season and avoiding the new lottery relegation zone. LaVine and Sabonis can aid in that, and doing so would also resuscitate their value and perhaps get them to more appealing situations while netting Sacramento trade assets in return. -- Slater

San Antonio Spurs
Can the Spurs live up to the hype?

San Antonio entered the 2025-26 season with the goal of earning a top-six seed for the postseason and shocked the NBA with a run to the Finals. Now, the Spurs head into 2026-27 with realistic title aspirations after finally breaking through a six-year playoff drought. Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs play in a league-high-tying 34 nationally televised games this season.

How will this still relatively inexperienced team handle the limelight? The front office displayed confidence in the group on hand by bringing in only one player (Tobias Harris) who will crack the rotation from last season. If Wembanyama continues on his trajectory, this could finally be his MVP season. -- Wright

Toronto Raptors
Is the Kawhi Leonard-Scottie Barnes pairing a home run?

The Raptors had good news and bad news after last season. They absolutely took a step forward, making the playoffs and taking the Cavs to seven games despite not having starters Immanuel Quickley or Brandon Ingram by the end. Barnes had a brilliant two-way season, maturing into the kind of force they always hoped he'd become.

But the bad news was Toronto had an expensive roster and it was not in a great position to improve it. Plus, there's a new controlling owner, Ed Rogers, and that sort of stuff gets everyone on edge. So the Raptors had to stick their necks out a little and take a risk and it, surprisingly, was the same risk they took in 2018 when they won the title: They traded for Leonard. Oh, and gave him a two-year, $115 million extension as he was stepping out of the cloud of a massive scandal in L.A.

The idea of Barnes and Leonard, who had a spectacular season in 2025-26, is delicious. Combining two two-way forwards with great size and scoring ability with young Collin Murray-Boyles could give the Raptors one of the best frontcourts in the league. Could. Counting on Leonard has been a fool's game this entire decade: Good luck to everyone involved! -- Windhorst

Utah Jazz
Can the Jazz make the massive leap to competitiveness?

After a painful rebuilding process, the Jazz plan to hit the gas this season, as president of basketball operations Austin Ainge put it. Utah has accumulated an intriguing collection of talent, but there will be some growing pains as the group learns to win in the NBA. Jaren Jackson Jr. is the team's only foundational player who has any playoff experience. -- MacMahon

Washington Wizards
What happens with Anthony Davis?
